description: We are a team of students united by our passion for space, technology, engineering, and innovation. We enjoy exploring new ideas, solving real-world challenges, and turning creative concepts into meaningful solutions. NASA Space Apps is an opportunity for us to learn, experiment, collaborate, and push our ideas further. We value curiosity, creativity, teamwork, and the willingness to learn from each other.
summary:
Before NASA builds bases on the Moon and Mars, every system must be tested somewhere, and testing on the Moon or Mars is costly, difficult and resource-heavy. That is why NASA needs Earth analogs, but the ones in use are few, repeated and hard to choose from.

UraNalog solves this. It is a web platform that uses open NASA and space-agency data to discover new analog sites on Earth whose conditions are close to a chosen Moon or Mars target. Scientists select the analog type, the target, the mission and the characteristics they need, and UraNalog ranks the best candidates, showing each site's characteristics and honest limits.

It puts everything in one place instead of scattered portals, and it is built to last: when data changes or new datasets appear, scientists can add them and keep building new analogs. The result is a clearer, faster way to choose the right analog, helping NASA save time and resources.
details:
How Does Our Solution Work

The scientist enters a simple guided workflow. First, they pick the type of terrain they need, such as desert, volcanic, polar or cave. Second, they choose the target, the Moon or Mars. Third, they choose the mission to test, such as a rover traverse, drilling for water ice or life detection. Fourth, they set what the place must be like, for example maximum slope, temperature and wind, and minimum sunlight or remoteness. UraNalog then searches open NASA and space-agency data and returns only the new sites that match, ranked, each with its characteristics and honest limits. An AI assistant on every page answers questions, and new data can be added at any time so new analogs keep being discovered.

When the search finishes, UraNalog shows the result as a ranked list of candidate sites, strongest to weakest, which can be viewed as cards, on a satellite map, or side by side for comparison. Each candidate opens into a profile with its location, a table comparing its characteristics (such as slope, sunlit fraction and temperature range) against what the mission needs, and the data source of every value. The engine gives a verdict (pass, borderline or excluded) with a confidence level, lists which Moon and Mars base operations the site can and cannot support, such as permafrost drilling, life-detection validation or EVA rehearsal, and states its limits, including values that rest only on proxy evidence and should be treated as provisional. From there, the scientist can inspect the site on the satellite map or ask the AI assistant about it.

The UraNalog benefits

Discovering new analogs and guiding users with an AI assistant that compares sites and cites the data behind every answer.
Putting all analogs in one place, with their characteristics, sources, and limits, instead of scattered portals.
Staying sustainable, as new data from NASA and partner agencies can be added over time.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:
TypeScript → for the website and user flow.
Python → for data processing and finding matching sites.
CSS → for styling and responsive design.


Tools:
Figma → for UI/UX design and Figma Make for inspiration.
React, Vite, Tailwind CSS → for building the web app.
Docker → for running the project the same way on any machine.
